02 · Polynomial logistic regression: approximation is not the problem (Figure 2)

Hypothesis H1. The mock paper's polynomial models fail because of sample complexity in the irrelevant coordinates, not because polynomials cannot represent the label function. Design. One controlled change at a time; everything else is identical to the mock paper (normalised PolynomialFeatures kernel, logistic loss, ||(C=0.85||)):
step input model / regulariser split
1. reproduction all ||(n||) bits mock paper's code, ||(C=0.85||) mock paper's split
2. intervention 1 the 10 selected bits same model, ||(C=0.85||) 5 stratified 60/20/20 splits
3. intervention 2 10 selected bits ||(C\in\{0.85,10,10^2,10^3,10^4\}||) chosen on validation data 5 splits
4. theory population infinite data, (almost) no regularisation —

Figure 2

Reading Figure 2. On all ||(n||) bits (grey) the mock paper's model stays near 55% at every degree, as the mock paper reports. Restricting the same model to the 10 selected coordinates lifts it to 83–90% at degree 10 even with the mock paper's strong regulariser, and to the Bayes level (~96%) once ||(C||) is chosen on validation data — from degree 6 on, exactly the polynomial-threshold degree of ||(f||) (notebook 01). The dotted line is the infinite-data limit. The mock paper's models failed for lack of data relative to the ||(\binom{n+d}{d}||)-dimensional feature space, not for lack of expressive power: H1 is supported.
